subtitle: The Cymaeans are ready to obey, but Aristodicus doubts the report and goes to ask the god again

notes.label: Aristodicus
notes.body: A citizen of Cyme, known only from this story; Herodotus names his father as Heraclides. His name is made from ἄριστος, "best", and δίκη, "justice".

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: ταῦτα comes first and points straight back to the oracle, so the reader sees the Cymaeans react at once.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.trans: they set about handing him over
notes.body: The Cymaeans move to obey immediately, which shows how ready they are to be rid of Pactyes.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.trans: they set about ... as they were setting about
notes.body: The same verb appears twice in different forms, which stresses how eager the people were and how close Pactyes came to being surrendered.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The crowd is set right next to a single named man, so the reader sees one citizen standing against the whole city.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Herodotus establishes Aristodicus' standing straight away, which explains how one man is able to stop a whole city.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The short, decisive verb shows Aristodicus acting on his own authority against the will of the majority.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: His disbelief is placed first in the explanation, which marks suspicion as the key to his character.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two reasons are linked with τε καί, which shows that his doubts are deliberate and thought through.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.quote: δοκῶν τοὺς θεοπρόπους οὐ λέγειν ἀληθῶς
notes.trans: thinking the envoys were not telling the truth
notes.body: He blames the envoys and leaves the god himself unquestioned, so he can resist the oracle while still appearing respectful.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: A blunt accusation against his own city's envoys, which shows how far he will go to avoid surrendering Pactyes.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The question is to be asked again, which prepares the reader for a test of the god.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.body: The future participle shows that the envoys set out with one purpose, so the reader expects a confrontation at the oracle.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.trans: of whom Aristodicus too was one
notes.body: His name comes at the end of the sentence, so the reader knows he is now the central character of the story.

questions: Why do you think Aristodicus blames the envoys rather than the oracle itself?
What does Herodotus tell us about Aristodicus that makes it believable that one man could stop a whole city?
